full_prose_under_review.title: Patient Counseling in Massachusetts: the Offer, the Counseling and the Record
full_prose_under_review.topic: Patient care / Patient counseling under 247 CMR 9.18 and M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: When counseling is owed and to whom, who may make the offer and who may deliver the counseling, the face-to-face and telephone offer methods and the off-site toll-free pathway, what the statute requires once the offer is accepted and what it says when the offer is declined, the designated consultation area and the counseling rights sign, counseling availability and the measuring device, and the refusal record together with the presumption that arises from its absence
learning_objectives: Separate the three Massachusetts counseling duties — the offer, the counseling itself and the record — and name the actor, the trigger and the consequence attached to each.

State the three different triggers that operate in this area: 247 CMR 9.18(1) on each person who receives a prescription medication, M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A on any person who presents a new prescription for filling, and 247 CMR 9.18(4) on each new drug therapy and each therapy significant for the patient's health and safety.

Apply the statutory offer methods in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A, confine the alternative-method exception to the ground the statute gives it, and state what the same section says about those methods for third party reimbursement and payment programs.
Distinguish who may extend the offer from who may deliver the counseling under 247 CMR 9.18(1) through (3), and place a pharmacy intern and a pharmacy technician correctly.

State what M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A requires once the offer to counsel is accepted and what the same section says about a person who declines it, and keep that disclaimer inside the section it is stated of.
Work 247 CMR 9.18(5) as a professional-judgment menu of what counseling may include rather than as a mandatory script.
Set the statutory counseling-content list in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A beside the regulatory list in 247 CMR 9.18(5) and say where the two are worded differently.
Apply the off-site delivery pathway in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A and state exactly where the toll-free service number must appear.

Test a consultation area against both the privacy condition and the access-route condition in 247 CMR 9.18(6), and a rights sign against the dimensions, letter height, placement and fixed wording in 247 CMR 9.18(7).
State the counseling-availability duty and the measuring-device duty in 247 CMR 9.18(8) and (9) without narrowing either one.
Apply the presumption that arises from the absence of a record of a failure to accept the offer, and say where that record may be kept.
Place the two inpatient carve-outs correctly, state each one's reservation in the terms its own text uses, and keep drug utilization review and the patient profile outside a counseling answer.

orientation.text: Massachusetts imposes three separate counseling duties, and almost every question in this area is decided by keeping them apart. The first is the offer. Under 247 CMR 9.18(1) a pharmacist or a pharmacist's designee shall offer the counseling services of the pharmacist to each person who receives a prescription medication, and under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A a pharmacist shall offer to counsel any person who presents a new prescription for filling. The second is the counseling itself, which under 247 CMR 9.18(3) shall be made by a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern, and which 247 CMR 9.18(4) requires on each new drug therapy and on each drug therapy that in the pharmacist's professional judgment is deemed to be significant for the health and safety of the patient. The third is the record, which M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A places on the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee and which carries an evidentiary consequence when it is silent. Three duties, three actors, three triggers; a fact pattern that satisfies one of them says nothing about the other two.

The offer is the widest of the three duties, and it is not the only one a person other than a pharmacist may touch: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A puts the reasonable efforts to obtain, record and maintain the patient information on the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee as well. What a designee may never do is counsel, which 247 CMR 9.18(3) confines to a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern. 247 CMR 9.18(1) lets a pharmacist's designee extend it, and 247 CMR 9.18(2) supplies the control on that delegation: a pharmacist shall ensure his or her designee is appropriately trained to make the offer to counsel. The regulation therefore constrains the designee through a training duty owed by the pharmacist rather than through a credential, which is why front-counter staff may make the offer and why no Board approval or licence class is the thing being tested. How the offer is made is fixed by statute rather than left to the pharmacy's convenience. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A provides that the offer shall be made either by face to face communication between the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee and the patient, or by telephone, except when the patient's needs or availability require an alternative method of counseling. The two named methods are the rule and the alternative is a needs-driven exception, so a line printed on a receipt inviting the patient to ask for the pharmacist is not the statutory offer, while an alternative method for a patient who cannot use a telephone is exactly what the exception is for.

The counseling itself is narrower in every direction. 247 CMR 9.18(3) states that counseling shall be made by a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern and that a pharmacy technician or other individual may not counsel any patient, so a pharmacy intern sits inside the permitted class and a pharmacy technician sits outside it however experienced or certified. The trigger in 247 CMR 9.18(4) has two limbs, and candidates lose the question by stopping at the first: counseling is required on each new drug therapy and on each drug therapy that in the pharmacist's professional judgment is deemed to be significant for the health and safety of the patient. Refill status therefore does not end the inquiry. What the counseling contains is then governed by 247 CMR 9.18(5) — and, in different words, by M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A, which carries a content list of its own. The regulation requires the pharmacist or pharmacy intern to provide such information as, in the pharmacist's professional judgment, is necessary for the patient to understand the proper use of the patient's prescription, and lists what that information may include: name, description and indication of the medication; dosage form, dosage, route of administration and duration of therapy; special directions and instructions for preparation, administration and use by the patient; common side and adverse effects or interactions and therapeutic contraindications or precautions with legend and non-legend medications and other substances the pharmacist deems relevant; techniques for self-monitoring drug therapy; proper storage and disposal; prescription refill information; and action to be taken in the event of a missed dose or adverse reaction. It is a professional-judgment menu, not a script, and it is clinical throughout.

The statute reaches the same encounter from the other end, and its terms decide the fact pattern candidates meet most often. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A provides that if an offer to provide counseling is accepted, the pharmacist shall counsel the person presenting the prescription to the extent the pharmacist deems appropriate, and it gives its own list of what such counseling may include, but not be limited to: the name and description of the medication; the dosage form, dosage, route of administration and duration of drug therapy; special instructions and precautions for preparation, administration and use by the patient; common adverse or severe side effects or interactions and therapeutic contraindications that may be encountered, including their avoidance and the action required if they occur; techniques for self-monitoring drug therapy; proper storage; prescription refill information; and action to be taken in the event of a missed dose. The paragraph that follows is the one a declined offer turns on: nothing in this section shall be construed to require a pharmacist to provide counseling if the person presenting the prescription declines to accept such offer for counseling. Read that disclaimer as it is written. It is stated of this section, meaning § 21A itself, so on the statute's own terms a declined offer leaves the pharmacist under no statutory duty to counsel that person; 247 CMR 9.18(4) addresses a pharmacist or pharmacy intern and states its trigger without any equivalent words, and says nothing express about a person who declines. What the statute does with a refusal is to make it the recordable event and then key its presumption to the absence of that record. One further sentence of § 21A belongs with the offer methods rather than with the counseling: for the purposes of medical assistance and other third party reimbursements or payment programs, any of the above methods, or a combination thereof, shall constitute an acceptable offer to provide counseling.

Three of the duties in 247 CMR 9.18 are things the pharmacy must have rather than things a pharmacist must say, and they are graded on the premises. 247 CMR 9.18(6) requires a designated patient consultation area, with signage stating Patient Consultation Area, designed to provide adequate privacy for confidential visual and auditory patient counseling, and then adds a second condition that a compliant-looking room can still fail: the private consultation area shall be accessible by a patient from the outside of the prescription dispensing area without having to traverse a stockroom or the prescription dispensing area. Privacy, signage wording and the access route are three separate tests of one space. 247 CMR 9.18(7) is prescriptive in a different way. It requires a sign of not less than 11 inches in height by 14 inches in width, in a conspicuous place adjacent to each area where prescriptions are dispensed, for the purpose of informing customers of their right to counseling by a pharmacist, in letters not less than one half inch in height, reading: Dear patients, you have the right to know about the proper use of your medication and its effects. If you need more information please ask the pharmacist. Adjacent to each dispensing area means two dispensing windows are two signs, and the size, the letter height, the placement and the wording are all separately prescribed.

Two further operational duties sit beside them and are routinely read too narrowly. Under 247 CMR 9.18(8) a pharmacy and pharmacist shall ensure counseling is available at all times when the pharmacy is open for business, so counseling availability tracks the pharmacy's own opening rather than the presence of any particular staff arrangement. Under 247 CMR 9.18(9) a pharmacy and pharmacist shall dispense or recommend a proper measuring device with all liquid medications, and the provision carries no paediatric qualifier, no prescription-only qualifier and no controlled-substance qualifier: all liquid medications means all of them, and the duty is satisfied either by dispensing the device or by recommending one. Both duties are addressed to the pharmacy and the pharmacist together, which is worth noticing in a fact pattern that tries to locate the failure in one or the other.

Delivery away from the pharmacy has its own pathway, and it is the one place in this area where the requirements are satisfied by a piece of infrastructure rather than by a conversation. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A provides that if a person elects delivery of a prescription drug at a location other than a pharmacy, the requirements of the section may be satisfied by providing that person with access to a toll-free telephone service to facilitate communication between the person and the pharmacist at the pharmacy. The sentence that follows is the one that decides questions: the number of that toll-free telephone service shall be printed on a label affixed to each container of a prescription drug dispensed by a pharmacy to a patient. Each container, and a label affixed to it. A number on the outer shipping carton, on the delivery receipt the patient signs, in the enclosed paperwork or in a message sent after the package arrives is not the specified placement, and the pharmacy's ordinary local number is not the specified service. Providing the access and printing the number are two steps, and a pharmacy that does the first without the second has not completed the pathway.

The record is a separate duty with its own actor and its own evidentiary consequence. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee shall make reasonable efforts to obtain, record and maintain specified patient information generated at an individual pharmacy, and that information includes any additional comments relevant to the patient's drug use, including any failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel. The refusal is therefore the event the statute asks the pharmacy to capture, and it is the same event the section's own disclaimer speaks to: a person who declines the offer is a person § 21A does not require the pharmacist to counsel. The statute is permissive about where the information lives: it may be recorded in the patient's manual or electronic profile, in the prescription signature log, or in any other system of records, so an answer that insists on the profile alone is too narrow. Then comes the provision that runs against the intuition candidates bring to documentation questions. The absence of any record of a failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel shall create a presumption that such counseling was provided. Silence therefore operates in the pharmacist's favour, and the statute nowhere asks for an affirmative note that counseling occurred; what it asks the pharmacy to capture is the refusal. The presumption is keyed only to the state of the refusal record, so a defect elsewhere in the section — a missing container legend, a badly placed sign — neither creates nor destroys it.

Two boundaries close the section. The first is the inpatient line, which Massachusetts draws twice and in different terms. 247 CMR 9.18(10) provides that the provisions of 247 CMR 9.18 do not apply to pharmacists while practising in an inpatient setting, unless otherwise required by law or regulation, so the carve-out is keyed to the practitioner and removes the whole section rather than merely the offer. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A draws its line by reference to the drug instead: the section does not apply to any drug dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home, except to the extent required by regulations promulgated by the Federal Health Care Financing Administration pursuant to the provisions of 42 USC 1396r-8. That reservation names one federal provision and reserves the regulations made under it; it is not a reference to federal regulation at large, and it is narrower than the formula 247 CMR 9.18(10) uses, which reaches anything otherwise required by law or regulation. The second boundary is subject matter. The prospective drug utilization review that M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A requires before a new prescription is dispensed, and the demographic and history items of the patient information the same statute enumerates, belong to a separate topic and are not taught here. What this section states about the general duty is the umbrella proposition in its own terms: a pharmacist must comply with the patient-counseling requirements of 247 CMR 9.18 in the settings and circumstances the regulation governs, applying any narrower setting-specific, product-specific or emergency exception before the general rule.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacy trains its front-counter clerks to make the offer to counsel at pickup so the pharmacist can stay at the verification station. One afternoon a clerk makes the offer on a new prescription, the patient accepts, and the patient's only question is what to do if she misses a dose. The clerk answers it from the leaflet and hands over the bag. The pharmacist-in-charge is satisfied, on the ground that the clerk was trained exactly as the regulation requires. Is the encounter compliant?
steps: Take the offer first. 247 CMR 9.18(1) allows a pharmacist or a pharmacist's designee to offer the counseling services of the pharmacist to each person who receives a prescription medication, so the clerk was a permissible person to make the offer.

Check the control on the delegation. 247 CMR 9.18(2) requires the pharmacist to ensure the designee is appropriately trained to make the offer to counsel, and the pharmacy has done that; the training duty is what the regulation imposes, not a credential.

Now identify what happened after the offer was accepted. Answering what to take on a missed dose is counseling content: 247 CMR 9.18(5)(h) lists action to be taken in the event of a missed dose or adverse reaction among the information counseling may include.

Apply the person limit to that act. 247 CMR 9.18(3) provides that counseling shall be made by a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern, and that a pharmacy technician or other individual may not counsel any patient. The clerk is an other individual.
Note that the training in 247 CMR 9.18(2) is expressly training to make the offer to counsel; it does not extend the class of persons who may counsel under 247 CMR 9.18(3).
worked_examples.resolution: The offer was properly made and the counseling was not. Once the patient accepted, the encounter had to pass to a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern. The error the scenario invites is treating the training duty in 247 CMR 9.18(2) as an authorisation that carries the designee across the line drawn by 247 CMR 9.18(3), so that the person permitted to extend the offer is assumed to be the person permitted to answer the question.

worked_examples.scenario: A chain configures its dispensing software so that the counseling prompt fires only on prescriptions the system flags as new, and is suppressed on every refill. The compliance manager explains that the regulation attaches the duty to new drug therapy, that refills by definition are not new, and that the pharmacy still posts its rights sign so any patient who wants counseling can ask. Evaluate the policy.
steps: Read 247 CMR 9.18(4) to the end. It requires counseling on each new drug therapy AND on each drug therapy that in the pharmacist's professional judgment is deemed to be significant for the health and safety of the patient.
Notice that the second limb is not keyed to the newness of the prescription at all. It is keyed to the significance of the therapy, assessed by the pharmacist, so a refill can sit squarely inside it.
Recognise that a software flag cannot perform the second limb, because the limb requires the pharmacist's professional judgment about this therapy and this patient.

Test the fallback the manager offers. The rights sign in 247 CMR 9.18(7) informs customers of their right to counseling by a pharmacist; it is a posting duty of the pharmacy and it does not convert the counseling duty into one that operates only on request.

Add the availability duty. Under 247 CMR 9.18(8) a pharmacy and pharmacist shall ensure counseling is available at all times when the pharmacy is open for business, which is a further reason the pharmacy cannot design the second limb out of its workflow.
worked_examples.resolution: The policy is defective because it implements only the first limb of 247 CMR 9.18(4). The error the scenario invites is reading new drug therapy as the whole trigger and treating refill status as an answer, when the professional-judgment limb reaches any therapy significant for the patient's health and safety whatever the fill number.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient presents a new prescription at a Massachusetts pharmacy. The pharmacist makes the offer to counsel face to face, and the patient says she has taken this medicine before, does not want to discuss it, and declines. The therapy is one the pharmacist would otherwise judge significant for her health and safety. The pharmacy's written policy says counseling is compulsory on every new prescription whatever the patient says, so a technician is told to keep her at the counter until the pharmacist has delivered it. A second pharmacist takes the opposite view, that once a patient declines there is nothing further the law asks of anyone. Work both positions.
steps: Start with the offer, which was owed whatever the answer turns out to be. 247 CMR 9.18(1) requires a pharmacist or a pharmacist's designee to offer the counseling services of the pharmacist to each person who receives a prescription medication, and M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A requires the pharmacist to offer to counsel any person who presents a new prescription for filling. The offer was made face to face, one of the two methods the statute names.

Take the statute's own answer to the declination. Nothing in § 21A shall be construed to require a pharmacist to provide counseling if the person presenting the prescription declines to accept such offer for counseling, so no statutory duty to counsel her arises on these facts.

Read the disclaimer no wider than its words. It is stated of this section, so it speaks to § 21A. 247 CMR 9.18(4) requires a pharmacist or pharmacy intern to provide counseling on each new drug therapy and on each drug therapy deemed significant for the health and safety of the patient, and states no equivalent disclaimer, so the regulation is not answered out of the statute's sentence.

Dispose of the first position. Neither text authorises holding a patient who has declined at the counter, and the statute says in terms that counseling is not required of the pharmacist on that footing.

Dispose of the second. A declination does not empty the encounter. The failure to accept is precisely what § 21A asks the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee to record, in the patient's manual or electronic profile, the prescription signature log or any other system of records, and it is the absence of such a record that would otherwise raise the presumption that counseling was provided.
worked_examples.resolution: Both positions overshoot. The statute answers the declination in terms, so the pharmacist is not required by § 21A to counsel a person who declines the offer, while the offer duty, the record of the failure to accept and the separately stated trigger in 247 CMR 9.18(4) all stay where they were. The error the scenario invites is taking one text as the whole law: reading 247 CMR 9.18(4) as a mandate that survives any refusal, or reading the statute's disclaimer as a discharge of everything else the encounter owed.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacy ships prescriptions to patients who elect home delivery. Its toll-free number reaches a pharmacist at the dispensing pharmacy during opening hours, and the number is printed prominently on the outside of the shipping carton and on the delivery receipt the courier collects. The pharmacy's records contain no entry showing that a particular patient failed to accept an offer to counsel. The general manager argues that because the counseling presumption runs in the pharmacy's favour, the labeling question is academic. Assess both issues.
steps: Confirm the pathway is available. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A permits the requirements of the section to be satisfied, where a person elects delivery at a location other than a pharmacy, by access to a toll-free telephone service facilitating communication with the pharmacist at the pharmacy.
Read the placement sentence exactly. The number of that toll-free telephone service shall be printed on a label affixed to each container of a prescription drug dispensed by a pharmacy to a patient.

Compare the facts. A carton is not a container of a prescription drug and a delivery receipt is not a label affixed to one, so the pharmacy has provided the access without completing the labeling step.

Turn to the second issue separately. The absence of any record of a failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel creates a presumption that such counseling was provided, and that presumption is keyed only to the state of the refusal record.
Refuse to let one issue decide the other. The presumption is not a general finding of compliance with M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A, and a labeling defect is not a record of a failure to accept.
worked_examples.resolution: The remote-delivery pathway is incomplete because the toll-free number is not on a label affixed to each container, and the presumption that counseling was provided nonetheless arises because no failure to accept is recorded. The error the scenario invites is the manager's: collapsing an operational requirement and an evidentiary presumption into a single compliance verdict, so that a favourable answer on one is taken to cure the other.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy with two dispensing windows at opposite ends of a long counter posts one 11 by 14 inch counseling rights sign, correctly worded and in half-inch letters, on the wall beside the store entrance. Its consultation room is fully enclosed, quiet, and signed Private Consultation Room, but the only door into it opens off the prescription dispensing area, so a patient is escorted behind the counter to reach it. The manager treats the room as the pharmacy's strongest compliance feature. List the defects.
steps: Start with the sign's placement. 247 CMR 9.18(7) requires the sign in a conspicuous place adjacent to each area where prescriptions are dispensed, so two dispensing windows are two areas and one sign at the entrance does not cover either of them.

Confirm what the sign does satisfy, because a defect list has to be accurate: the dimensions of not less than 11 inches by 14 inches, the letter height of not less than one half inch and the prescribed wording are all met.

Turn to the room and separate the two conditions in 247 CMR 9.18(6). The first is a designated patient consultation area designed to provide adequate privacy for confidential visual and auditory patient counseling, which the enclosed quiet room meets.

Apply the second condition, which is about the route rather than the room. The private consultation area shall be accessible by a patient from the outside of the prescription dispensing area without having to traverse a stockroom or the prescription dispensing area, and an escort behind the counter is exactly the traverse the regulation forbids.
Check the room's signage against the regulation's own words. 247 CMR 9.18(6) calls for signage stating Patient Consultation Area, so Private Consultation Room is not the prescribed designation.
worked_examples.resolution: There are three defects: the rights sign is not posted adjacent to each dispensing area, the consultation area cannot be reached without traversing the prescription dispensing area, and its signage does not state Patient Consultation Area. The error the scenario invites is grading each feature on the impression it makes — a large correct sign, a genuinely private room — rather than on the placement, access and wording conditions that 247 CMR 9.18(6) and (7) state separately.

worked_examples.scenario: During an inspection a pharmacist is asked to show that a patient was counseled on a prescription dispensed seven months earlier. The pharmacy's records contain no note that counseling was given and no note that the patient declined it. The pharmacist assumes the worst, on the footing that a documentation question with nothing in the file must go against the pharmacy, and prepares to concede the point. Is that concession correct?
steps: Identify what M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A actually asks the pharmacy to record. The pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee shall make reasonable efforts to obtain, record and maintain patient information including any failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel.
Notice what the statute does not ask for. It does not require an affirmative entry that counseling was provided; the recordable event it names on this point is the refusal.
Apply the presumption in its own terms. The absence of any record of a failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel shall create a presumption that such counseling was provided.
Match it to the facts. There is no record of a failure to accept, so the presumption arises and it runs in the pharmacist's favour rather than against him.

Keep the scope of the presumption honest. It speaks to whether counseling was provided; it does not certify that the offer was made by a statutory method or that any other requirement of the section was met.
worked_examples.resolution: The concession is wrong. On these facts the presumption that counseling was provided arises from the silence of the refusal record. The error the scenario invites is importing the ordinary recordkeeping intuition that an undocumented act is an unperformed act, when this statute reverses it by keying the presumption to the absence of a refusal entry.

retrieval_prompts.answer: A pharmacist; a pharmacy intern; a pharmacy technician or other individual.

247 CMR 9.18(2): a pharmacist shall ensure his or her designee is appropriately trained to make the offer to counsel; the control is a training duty on the pharmacist, not a credential on the designee.
247 CMR 9.18(3): counseling shall be made by a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern, and a pharmacy technician or other individual may not counsel any patient.

247 CMR 9.18(4): a pharmacist or pharmacy intern shall provide counseling on each new drug therapy and on each drug therapy that in the pharmacist's professional judgment is deemed significant for the health and safety of the patient.

decision_logic.condition: A person is receiving a prescription medication at the pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Make the offer under 247 CMR 9.18(1). A pharmacist or a pharmacist's designee may make it, provided the pharmacist has ensured the designee is appropriately trained to make the offer to counsel.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription the person presents for filling is a new prescription.
decision_logic.action: The statutory offer duty in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A attaches as well. Make the offer by face to face communication or by telephone, and use an alternative method only where the patient's needs or availability require it.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription is a refill and the therapy is not new.
decision_logic.action: Do not stop there. Apply the second limb of 247 CMR 9.18(4) and ask whether this drug therapy is, in the pharmacist's professional judgment, significant for the health and safety of the patient.

decision_logic.condition: The person accepts the offer to counsel.
decision_logic.action: Counsel the person presenting the prescription to the extent you deem appropriate under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A, drawing on that section's list and on the 247 CMR 9.18(5) list as professional judgment makes necessary for the patient to understand proper use.

decision_logic.condition: Counseling is to be provided, whether because the offer was accepted or because 247 CMR 9.18(4) is engaged.
decision_logic.action: Hand the encounter to a pharmacist or a pharmacy intern. A pharmacy technician or other individual may not counsel any patient, and training to make the offer does not change that.

decision_logic.condition: You are deciding what the counseling should cover.
decision_logic.action: Provide what professional judgment makes necessary for the patient to understand proper use of the prescription, drawing on the 247 CMR 9.18(5) list of clinical items rather than reciting it or adding commercial information to it.

decision_logic.condition: The person elects delivery of the prescription drug at a location other than a pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Provide access to a toll-free telephone service facilitating communication with the pharmacist at the pharmacy, and print that number on a label affixed to each container. Both steps are required; neither substitutes for the other.

decision_logic.condition: The person declines the offer to counsel.
decision_logic.action: Record the failure to accept as part of the reasonable efforts to obtain, record and maintain patient information; the profile, the prescription signature log or any other system of records will do. Then note what M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A says for itself: nothing in that section shall be construed to require a pharmacist to provide counseling if the person presenting the prescription declines to accept the offer. 247 CMR 9.18(4) states its own trigger without equivalent words, so do not answer for the regulation out of the statute's disclaimer.

decision_logic.condition: You are asked whether counseling was provided on a past fill and the file is silent.
decision_logic.action: Look specifically for a record of a failure to accept the offer. Its absence creates the presumption that counseling was provided, so do not concede the point for want of an affirmative note.

decision_logic.condition: You are auditing the pharmacy's premises for counseling compliance.
decision_logic.action: Test the consultation area for privacy, for the Patient Consultation Area signage and for the access route; then test the rights sign for its dimensions, letter height, conspicuous placement adjacent to each dispensing area and prescribed wording.

decision_logic.condition: A liquid medication is being dispensed, or the pharmacy is setting its opening hours and staffing.
decision_logic.action: Dispense or recommend a proper measuring device whatever the patient's age, and ensure counseling is available at all times when the pharmacy is open for business.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacist is practising in an inpatient setting, or the drug is dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home.
decision_logic.action: Apply the carve-outs before the general rule: 247 CMR 9.18 does not apply to pharmacists practising in an inpatient setting unless otherwise required by law or regulation, and M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A does not apply to such a drug except to the extent required by regulations promulgated by the Federal Health Care Financing Administration pursuant to the provisions of 42 USC 1396r-8.

decision_logic.condition: The facts are about screening the prescription rather than about talking to the patient or recording the encounter.
decision_logic.action: Recognise that as prospective drug utilization review and the patient profile, a separate topic, and do not answer it out of 247 CMR 9.18 or out of the counseling paragraphs of M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A.

ma_vs_federal.text: No federal counseling rule is among this section's dependencies, so no federal counseling standard is stated here. The only federal reference inside the declared scope is a carve-back, and it is a narrow one: M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A withdraws its own inpatient exclusion to the extent required by regulations promulgated by the Federal Health Care Financing Administration pursuant to the provisions of 42 USC 1396r-8. What those regulations themselves require is not stated here.

247 CMR 9.18(10) uses a wider formula for the same idea, disapplying the section to pharmacists practising in an inpatient setting unless otherwise required by law or regulation, which reaches other law as well as federal regulation.

forms_records.text: The record that matters most in this area is the record of a failure to accept the pharmacist's offer to counsel, which sits inside the patient information the pharmacist or designee must make reasonable efforts to obtain, record and maintain.
Any additional comments relevant to the patient's drug use fall inside the same body of information to be obtained, recorded and maintained.

The permitted locations are stated in the alternative: the patient's manual or electronic profile, the prescription signature log, or any other system of records. An answer confined to the patient profile is too narrow.

The statute attaches an evidentiary consequence to the state of that record rather than to its contents: absence of any record of a failure to accept creates a presumption that counseling was provided, and no affirmative note that counseling occurred is required to raise it.

On the off-site delivery route the record-bearing artefact is the container label itself, which must carry the number of the toll-free telephone service on each container of a prescription drug dispensed to the patient.

Two postings are themselves prescribed records of a kind: signage stating Patient Consultation Area at the designated consultation area, and the counseling rights sign with its prescribed size, letter height, placement and wording.
For the designee the regulation states a training duty on the pharmacist rather than a form: the pharmacist shall ensure his or her designee is appropriately trained to make the offer to counsel.

The 247 CMR 9.18(5) list is not a checklist to be completed and filed. It describes information the pharmacist or intern may provide as professional judgment requires, so a completed form is not what demonstrates compliance with it.

The enumerated contents of the patient profile itself, and the prospective drug utilization review that precedes dispensing, are recordkeeping subjects belonging to a separate topic and are not stated here.

common_traps.text: Treating the offer and the counseling as one duty, so that a trained designee's authority to extend the offer is read as authority to counsel. 247 CMR 9.18(3) bars a pharmacy technician or other individual from counseling any patient.

Stopping at the first limb of 247 CMR 9.18(4) and concluding that a refill can never require counseling, when the professional-judgment limb reaches any therapy significant for the patient's health and safety.

Answering a declined-offer fact pattern out of 247 CMR 9.18(4) alone. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A says in terms that nothing in that section shall be construed to require a pharmacist to counsel a person who declines the offer.
Reading that disclaimer as a general licence. It is stated of M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A, and it does not touch the offer duty in 247 CMR 9.18(1) or the duty to record the failure to accept.
Treating the 247 CMR 9.18(5) list as a mandatory script, or expecting commercial information such as acquisition cost to sit inside a list that is clinical throughout.

Reading the patient's needs or availability exception in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A as making any method of offer acceptable at the pharmacy's convenience, rather than as a departure the patient's own circumstances must require.
Treating 247 CMR 9.18(5) as the only statement of what counseling may contain, when M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A carries a list of its own in different words.

Treating the toll-free number as satisfied by the outer shipping package, the delivery receipt, the enclosed paperwork or a message after delivery, when the statute specifies a label affixed to each container.
Assuming the counseling rights sign is a once-per-store requirement. It is required adjacent to each area where prescriptions are dispensed.
Checking only the size of the rights sign. The minimum dimensions, the minimum letter height, the conspicuous placement and the prescribed wording are all separately stated.

Grading a consultation area on privacy alone. A fully enclosed room still fails if the patient cannot reach it without traversing a stockroom or the prescription dispensing area, or if its signage does not state Patient Consultation Area.
Narrowing the measuring-device duty to paediatric liquids, when 247 CMR 9.18(9) reaches all liquid medications and is satisfied by dispensing or by recommending a proper device.
Reading the inpatient carve-out in 247 CMR 9.18(10) as removing only the offer, when it disapplies the provisions of 247 CMR 9.18 as a whole unless otherwise required by law or regulation.

Assuming an unrecorded encounter means counseling cannot be shown, or that the presumption depends on an affirmative record that counseling occurred. It is the absence of a record of a failure to accept that raises it.
Restricting the permitted record to the patient profile, when the prescription signature log and any other system of records are equally available.

Letting a defect in one duty decide another: a labeling failure on the off-site route neither creates nor destroys the record-based presumption, and the presumption is not a general certificate of compliance.

Substituting a general meaningful-offer formula for the terms Massachusetts actually uses. The regulation requires the offer of the pharmacist's counseling services to each person who receives a prescription medication, and the statute fixes the methods by which the offer is made.
Answering a counseling question out of the prospective drug utilization review or the patient profile requirements, which are a separate topic with their own trigger.

Reading the statutory inpatient reservation as any applicable federal regulation, when M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21A reserves regulations promulgated by the Federal Health Care Financing Administration pursuant to 42 USC 1396r-8.

orientation.text: Massachusetts puts the dispensing label on a statutory footing rather than leaving it to professional judgment. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21 the pharmacist filling a written, electronic or oral prescription for a controlled substance shall package the controlled substance in a container, affixing to the container a label showing the date of filling, the pharmacy name and address, the filling pharmacist's initials, the serial number of the prescription, the name of the patient unless it is a veterinary prescription, the name of the prescribing practitioner, the name of the controlled substance, directions for use and cautionary statements, if any, contained in such prescription or required by law, and, if the controlled substance is dispensed as tablets or capsules, the number of same in such container. That list is the pharmacist's list and it is the label's list. What the practitioner has to put on the face of the prescription is a separate subject with a separate provision, and the prescribing practitioner's registration number is not among the elements § 21 requires the pharmacist to show on the container.

Two features of § 21 are easy to miss because the section sits inside the Controlled Substances Act. The first is its reach. A later paragraph of § 21 provides that the labeling provisions of this section shall apply to the compounding and dispensing of drugs on the oral, electronic or written prescription of a licensed and registered prescriber under section 9, so the element list is not confined to controlled substances alone and a candidate who treats it as a controlled-substance-only list is reading the section too narrowly. The second is that the same section also carries provisions about the labeling of compounded drug preparations and about a pharmacy contact telephone number for compounding pharmacies. Those belong to compounding practice, they have their own canonical rule, and they are outside the scope declared for this section.

The accessibility duty in the second paragraph of § 21 is triggered by a request and by nothing else. Upon the request of an elderly person, as defined in section fourteen of chapter nineteen A, or of a person visually impaired, directions on the label affixed by the pharmacist to a container of a prescription drug shall be typed in a print size allowing no more than ten characters per inch. Three things in that sentence do all the work. The trigger is the request, so a patient who is plainly elderly but says nothing is owed nothing on this basis and a pharmacist has no duty to estimate age or eyesight. The standard is a ceiling on how many characters may be crowded into an inch rather than a floor on point size, so a label printed at twelve characters per inch fails and one at eight satisfies it. And what has to be enlarged is the directions, not the entire label.

How the label is produced is a regulatory question rather than a statutory one. 247 CMR 9.04(3) provides that a licensee shall ensure the label affixed to a prescription drug container or package is clearly printed by a computerized pharmacy system, and that in the event of printing or equipment failure a prescription label may be legibly handwritten or typed during an emergency period. The alternative carries two conditions, and legibility is not one of them. It opens in the event of printing or equipment failure, and it lasts during an emergency period, so it is contingent on a failure and bounded by the life of that failure. Legibility is what the substitute label must be once the exception is open; it is not what opens it. A queue, a staffing shortage or a settled preference for handwriting is not a printing or equipment failure, and a handwritten label produced after the equipment has been repaired sits outside the exception however carefully it is written. Note also that 9.04(3) speaks of a prescription drug container or package and is not limited to controlled substances.

The dispensing record has to capture what product actually went out of the door, and 247 CMR 9.04(7) states an ordered chain rather than a menu of acceptable identifiers. Whenever a prescription drug has been distributed solely under a generic name, the dispensing pharmacist shall record the NDC number in the computerized pharmacy system. In the event an NDC number does not exist, the pharmacist shall record the name of the manufacturer, or, if the manufacturer's name is not available, the name of the distributor, packer, or repacker. Each step becomes available only once the step above it is unavailable, so a pharmacist who can read the manufacturer's name off the carton does not get to record the repacker instead because the invoice happens to be closer to hand. Two boundaries follow from the same sentence. The trigger is distribution solely under a generic name, so a product distributed under a brand name never sets the paragraph running. And the destination is the computerized pharmacy system, so a note on a paper worksheet does not discharge a duty aimed at that system.

247 CMR 9.04(8) names who may take a new prescription over the telephone, and the answer is neither of the two that candidates reach for first. A pharmacy intern, or certified pharmacy technician who has the approval of the pharmacist on duty may receive new prescriptions over the telephone from a prescriber or authorized agent. So the pharmacist is not the only permissible recipient, and it is equally wrong to say that any member of staff may take the call. Inside that paragraph the technician limb carries two conditions that have to be satisfied together: the technician must be certified, and the technician must have the approval of the pharmacist on duty. An authorisation issued by a pharmacy manager who is not the pharmacist on duty is not the approval the paragraph names, and a pharmacist who reviews the transcription after the call has ended has not supplied an approval the technician needed in order to receive the call in the first place. The intern limb is stated in 9.04(8) without that qualifier, although 247 CMR 8.01(3) requires a pharmacy intern to work under the direct supervision of a registered pharmacist preceptor, so an intern is never an unsupervised recipient.

What 247 CMR 9.04(8) does not do is settle the question on its own, because the Board regulates the same act a second time and the Legislature reaches it as well. 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) provides that a certified pharmacy technician, after identifying him or herself as such, may request refill authorizations from the prescriber or prescriber's agent and, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, receive new or omitted prescription information from the prescriber or agent, except where otherwise prohibited by federal or state laws and regulations. Two things follow. The technician limb carries a condition 9.04(8) never states, namely that the technician identify him or herself as a certified pharmacy technician to the person on the other end of the line. And the grant is expressly subject to any other federal or state law or regulation prohibiting the act, so certification, self-identification and the on-duty pharmacist's approval are not the end of the inquiry. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 20(a) is the state law that most often carries it further: upon receiving an oral prescription for a controlled substance from an authorized practitioner, the pharmacist shall immediately reduce the prescription to writing on a prescription form and shall record the information the subsection enumerates. The statute addresses the pharmacist as the person who, on receiving such a prescription, reduces it to writing and records that information, so an oral controlled-substance prescription is not a call to hand on under 9.04(8) without working § 20(a) and the 8.04(4)(c) reservation first. One further category is named expressly: under 247 CMR 8.03(4)(c) a pharmacy technician trainee may not take prescriptions over the telephone at all.

Two things travel with a controlled substance at the counter, and they have different triggers and very different exception structures. The pamphlet comes first. Under § 21 the department, in consultation with relevant stakeholders and experts in the treatment and management of acute and chronic pain, produces and distributes, either in written or electronic form, to pharmacies, not including institutional pharmacies, consumer pamphlets covering pain management and the use and availability of non-opioid alternatives, the consumer's option to fill a schedule II prescription in a lesser quantity than indicated on the prescription, misuse and abuse of narcotics by adults and children, the risk of dependency and addiction, proper storage and disposal, addiction support and treatment resources, the bureau of substance addiction services telephone helpline, the risks of unintended overdose, and risk reduction measures. That lesser-quantity item is a topic the pamphlet must cover; the quantity rule itself is a separate subject and is not taught here. A pharmacist shall distribute the pamphlet when dispensing a narcotic or controlled substance contained in schedule II or III, and pharmacists shall not be required to distribute it if the patient is receiving outpatient palliative care pursuant to section 227 of chapter 111, the patient is a resident of a long-term care facility, or the narcotic or controlled substance is prescribed for use in the treatment of substance use disorder or opioid dependence. The first of those exceptions carries a cross-reference, and the cross-reference is what fixes the palliative care the exception means: care pursuant to section 227 of chapter 111, rather than outpatient palliative care at large.

The second thing owed at the counter is a conversation and an offer, and it sits in a different section that states no exceptions at all. M.G.L. c. 94C, § 18D(a) defines opioid antagonist as any drug approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of persons experiencing an opioid overdose. Section 18D(b) then provides that a pharmacist dispensing an opioid contained in Schedule II of section 3 shall inform the patient on the potential adverse risks of the prescription opioid and shall offer to dispense an opioid antagonist to the patient, and where applicable, to a designee of the patient, or for a patient who is a minor, to the minor's parent or guardian. Three readings have to be resisted. The duty is to offer, not to secure acceptance, so a patient who declines has not defeated it and dispensing the opioid is not made conditional on taking an antagonist. The duty belongs to the pharmacist who dispenses and is not conditioned on the prescriber having separately ordered an antagonist. And a minor patient does not make the offer disappear; it routes the offer to the parent or guardian. Section 18D states no exception for a patient who already keeps an antagonist at home and none for an experienced opioid user.

The pamphlet duty and the § 18D duties overlap on Schedule II, but they are not one duty and their exceptions do not travel between them. Every dispensing of a Schedule II opioid falls inside both triggers, because such a product is a controlled substance contained in schedule II and it is an opioid contained in Schedule II. Yet a patient receiving outpatient palliative care, a resident of a long-term care facility, and a patient whose Schedule II opioid is prescribed for the treatment of substance use disorder or opioid dependence each sit inside a stated exception to the pamphlet and inside no exception whatsoever to § 18D. A dispensing can therefore be one where no pamphlet is required and the adverse-risk information and the antagonist offer are still owed in full. The converse holds as well: a narcotic in Schedule III is inside the pamphlet trigger and outside § 18D, which reaches an opioid contained in Schedule II.

Three boundaries around this material are worth fixing before working any question. Both 247 CMR 9.04(3) and 247 CMR 9.04(7) point at the computerized pharmacy system, but the equipment and the premises are a separate subject: automated dispensing devices, pharmacy processing automation, processing performed outside the licensed pharmacy premises, and compliance packaging and storage equipment are governed elsewhere and nothing here decides any question about them. Only three paragraphs of 247 CMR 9.04 are taught in this section. The rest of that regulation carries its own canonical rules covering, among other things, bed-side delivery of discharge prescriptions, how the days of a prescription's validity period are counted, the validity of a Schedule VI prescription, positive identification of the person to whom a controlled substance is dispensed, and the disapplication of named paragraphs of 247 CMR 9.04 to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies; each of those has to be worked from its own provision rather than inferred from this section. The same holds for the rest of 247 CMR 8.04(4), which is used here only for what it says about receiving prescription information: a certified pharmacy technician's authority to perform prescription transfers between pharmacies for Schedule VI controlled substances only, and the acts 247 CMR 8.04(4)(e) closes to a certified technician, are neighbours of that paragraph and are worked from their own provisions. And the label rules taught here are about what the label carries and how it is produced; the counselling that accompanies a dispensing rests on a different statute and belongs to a different section.
