worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacist is filling a written prescription for a controlled substance dispensed as capsules. The pharmacy's label printer has failed and a technician has prepared a neat handwritten label. The patient collecting it is eighty-four and says nothing about the label; the patient behind her in the queue asks for larger directions because of impaired vision. The pharmacist proposes to enlarge the whole label for the eighty-four year old because she is plainly elderly, to leave the second patient's label in the pharmacy's standard size until a prescriber orders otherwise, and to keep writing labels by hand into next week because the handwriting is clear.
steps: Fix the label content first, because M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21 settles it independently of how the label is produced: the date of filling, the pharmacy name and address, the filling pharmacist's initials, the serial number of the prescription, the patient's name, the prescribing practitioner's name, the name of the controlled substance, directions for use and cautionary statements, and, the product being dispensed as capsules, the number of capsules in the container.

Test the handwritten label against 247 CMR 9.04(3). The label must be clearly printed by a computerized pharmacy system, and a legibly handwritten or typed label is permitted in the event of printing or equipment failure and during an emergency period. The printer has failed, so the exception is open while that failure lasts.

Separate legibility from the trigger. Clear handwriting is what the substitute label must be once the exception is open; it is not what opens the exception. Carrying the practice into next week, after the equipment has been repaired, puts the labels outside 247 CMR 9.04(3) no matter how neat they are.

Take the two accessibility questions as they were actually raised. The second paragraph of § 21 operates upon the request of an elderly person, as defined in section fourteen of chapter nineteen A, or of a person visually impaired. The eighty-four year old made no request, so the paragraph gives the pharmacist nothing to do for her.

Apply the standard to the patient who did ask. Her directions, and not her whole label, shall be typed in a print size allowing no more than ten characters per inch, and the statute conditions that on her request rather than on any order from a prescriber.
worked_examples.resolution: The handwritten label is permissible while the printer is down and impermissible once it is repaired; the eighty-four year old is owed nothing on this basis until she asks; and the patient who asked is owed enlarged directions on her own request, with no prescriber involved. The scenario invites three errors at once: reading legibility as the whole test in 247 CMR 9.04(3), making the § 21 accessibility duty automatic on apparent age, and enlarging the entire label instead of the directions.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacist fills two prescriptions in the same batch. The first product has been distributed solely under its generic name and carries no NDC number; the manufacturer's name is printed on the carton and the repacker's name appears on the wholesaler's invoice. The second product was distributed under a brand name and carries an NDC number on the package. The pharmacist proposes to note the repacker for the first product and the NDC for the second on a paper batch worksheet kept in the dispensary, on the view that the point of the rule is simply to identify what was dispensed.
steps: Test each product against the trigger in 247 CMR 9.04(7), which runs whenever a prescription drug has been distributed solely under a generic name. The first product meets it. The second, distributed under a brand name, does not, so the paragraph never starts running for it.

Work the first product down the chain in the order the paragraph sets. The pharmacist records the NDC number; in the event an NDC number does not exist, the name of the manufacturer; and, if the manufacturer's name is not available, the name of the distributor, packer, or repacker.

Apply that ordering to these facts. No NDC number exists, so the second step is reached. The manufacturer's name is available on the carton, so the third step is never reached and the repacker's name is not the entry the paragraph calls for.

Check where the entry has to go. 247 CMR 9.04(7) directs the record into the computerized pharmacy system, so a paper batch worksheet kept in the dispensary is not the record the paragraph requires, however carefully it is maintained.
worked_examples.resolution: The manufacturer's name goes into the computerized pharmacy system for the first product, and 247 CMR 9.04(7) requires nothing at all for the second. The scenario invites two errors: flattening an ordered fallback chain into a free choice among identifiers, and satisfying a requirement aimed at the computerized pharmacy system with a paper note.

worked_examples.scenario: A prescriber's office telephones a Massachusetts pharmacy with new prescriptions during a busy afternoon. The pharmacy manager, who is not the pharmacist on duty, has issued a written policy stating that any technician on staff may take new prescription calls so that the pharmacist is not interrupted. On this afternoon an uncertified technician takes the first call, a certified technician who has never raised the subject with the pharmacist on duty, and who does not identify herself as a certified pharmacy technician to the caller, takes the second, and a pharmacy intern takes the third. The pharmacist on duty reads all three transcriptions at the end of the shift and initials them. None of the three prescriptions is for a controlled substance.
steps: Read 247 CMR 9.04(8) as written: a pharmacy intern, or certified pharmacy technician who has the approval of the pharmacist on duty may receive new prescriptions over the telephone from a prescriber or authorized agent. Two categories of person are named, and no third.

Dispose of the uncertified technician first. Certification is a condition of the technician limb, so a technician who is not certified is not within the paragraph at all, and a manager's policy cannot put her there.

Take the certified technician next. Certification alone is not the whole limb; the paragraph adds the approval of the pharmacist on duty. A written authorisation from a pharmacy manager who is not the pharmacist on duty is not the approval the paragraph names.

Add the condition 247 CMR 9.04(8) never states. 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) permits a certified pharmacy technician to receive new or omitted prescription information from the prescriber or agent only after identifying him or herself as such, and this technician did not.

Ask whether the end-of-shift review cures anything. The paragraph conditions who may receive the call, so a review conducted after the prescription has already been taken does not convert an unauthorised receipt into an authorised one.

Finish with the intern. The intern limb of 247 CMR 9.04(8) is stated without the approval qualifier, so the pharmacy intern who took the third call is squarely within it, and 247 CMR 8.01(3) has the intern working under the direct supervision of a registered pharmacist preceptor in any event.
worked_examples.resolution: Only the intern's call was properly taken: the uncertified technician failed the certification condition and the certified technician failed the approval condition. The scenario invites the two errors the paragraph exists to catch, namely assuming that no one but a pharmacist may take a new telephoned prescription, and assuming that any technician may, with a later pharmacist check standing in for the approval the paragraph requires. Had any of the three been an oral prescription for a controlled substance, the analysis would have had further to run: 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) grants its authority except where otherwise prohibited by federal or state laws and regulations, and M.G.L. c. 94C, § 20(a) addresses the pharmacist as the person who, upon receiving such a prescription, shall immediately reduce it to writing.

worked_examples.scenario: A prescriber's agent telephones a Massachusetts pharmacy with a new oral prescription for a controlled substance. The pharmacist on duty is verifying another prescription and asks a certified pharmacy technician to take it. The technician holds a current certification, has the approval of the pharmacist on duty for telephone calls of this kind, and identifies herself as a certified pharmacy technician when she picks up. She writes the prescription out and puts it in the queue. The pharmacy's standing guidance says that because 247 CMR 9.04(8) lets a certified technician with the pharmacist's approval receive new prescriptions over the telephone, nothing further needs checking. Evaluate the guidance.
steps: Start where the guidance starts and confirm what 247 CMR 9.04(8) does say. A pharmacy intern, or certified pharmacy technician who has the approval of the pharmacist on duty may receive new prescriptions over the telephone from a prescriber or authorized agent, and on these facts both conditions in the technician limb are met.

Read the Board's other provision on the same act. 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) permits a certified pharmacy technician, after identifying him or herself as such and with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, to receive new or omitted prescription information from the prescriber or agent. The self-identification condition is satisfied here too.

Do not stop at the conditions, because the paragraph does not stop there. The same sentence grants that authority except where otherwise prohibited by federal or state laws and regulations, so a prohibition found elsewhere in state or federal law closes the grant however well the conditions inside the paragraph are met.

Go looking for the other law the reservation points at. What was telephoned is an oral prescription for a controlled substance, and M.G.L. c. 94C, § 20(a) provides that upon receiving an oral prescription for a controlled substance from an authorized practitioner, the pharmacist shall immediately reduce the prescription to writing on a prescription form and shall record the practitioner's name, address and registration number and the rest of the information the subsection enumerates.

Name the defect in the guidance rather than in the technician. The guidance treats 247 CMR 9.04(8) as the whole law on who takes the call, when a second regulation governs the same act with a further condition and an express reservation, and a statute addresses the pharmacist on an oral controlled-substance prescription.
worked_examples.resolution: The guidance is wrong to stop at 247 CMR 9.04(8). Every condition that paragraph names was met, and so was the self-identification condition 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) adds, but that paragraph grants its authority except where otherwise prohibited by federal or state laws and regulations, and a telephoned oral prescription for a controlled substance is where M.G.L. c. 94C, § 20(a) has to be worked: it addresses the pharmacist as the person who, upon receiving such a prescription, shall immediately reduce it to writing and record the enumerated information. The error the scenario invites is treating one paragraph as settling an act that several provisions govern.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacist has two Schedule II opioid prescriptions to dispense. The first is for an adult patient who is receiving outpatient palliative care pursuant to section 227 of chapter 111, and the pharmacist has correctly concluded that no consumer education pamphlet is required. The second is for a fifteen year old, and the patient's mother is collecting it. The pharmacist reasons that because the pamphlet duty falls away for the palliative care patient, the rest of the opioid education requirements fall away with it, and that an opioid antagonist cannot be dispensed to a minor, so nothing further is owed on the second prescription either.
steps: Confirm the pamphlet conclusion on the first prescription. A pharmacist shall distribute the pamphlet when dispensing a narcotic or controlled substance contained in schedule II or III, and pharmacists shall not be required to distribute it where the patient is receiving outpatient palliative care pursuant to section 227 of chapter 111. That stated exception is satisfied.

Refuse to carry the exception across. The pamphlet exceptions sit in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21 and govern the pamphlet. The adverse-risk information and the antagonist offer sit in M.G.L. c. 94C, § 18D(b), which states no exception for outpatient palliative care or for anything else.

State what is still owed on the first prescription. A pharmacist dispensing an opioid contained in Schedule II shall inform the patient on the potential adverse risks of the prescription opioid and shall offer to dispense an opioid antagonist, an opioid antagonist being any drug approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of persons experiencing an opioid overdose.

Turn to the minor. Section 18D(b) directs the offer to the patient and, where applicable, to a designee of the patient, or, for a patient who is a minor, to the minor's parent or guardian. Minority routes the offer rather than removing it, so on these facts the offer is made to the mother.

Work the pamphlet question on the second prescription separately. It is a dispensing of a controlled substance contained in schedule II, so the pamphlet duty is triggered unless one of the three stated exceptions is established, and nothing in these facts establishes one.
worked_examples.resolution: The palliative care patient is owed the adverse-risk information and the antagonist offer notwithstanding the pamphlet exception, and the minor's mother is owed the offer as the parent collecting the medication. The scenario invites the error of treating two duties triggered by the same dispensing as a single package, so that an exception written for one is read across to the other, with the further error of reading a patient's minority as a reason the offer disappears rather than as the reason it is directed elsewhere.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name every item M.G.L. c. 94C, § 21 requires the pharmacist to show on the container label of a filled controlled-substance prescription.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The date of filling; the pharmacy name and address; the filling pharmacist's initials; the serial number of the prescription; the name of the patient, unless it is a veterinary prescription; the name of the prescribing practitioner; the name of the controlled substance; directions for use and cautionary statements, if any, contained in the prescription or required by law; and, where the substance is dispensed as tablets or capsules, the number of them in the container.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the prescribing practitioner's registration number is one of the label elements § 21 enumerates.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. Section 21 requires the name of the prescribing practitioner. The registration number is not among the elements the pharmacist's container label must show.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which element of the § 21 label list is stated with an express 'unless', and what is it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The name of the patient, which is required unless it is a veterinary prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.04(3) a prescription label must be ______, and a handwritten or typed label is permitted only ______ and only ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: clearly printed by a computerized pharmacy system; in the event of printing or equipment failure; during an emergency period.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacy writes labels legibly by hand on a busy Monday while the printer is working normally. Is that within 247 CMR 9.04(3)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Legibility is what the substitute label must be, not what makes the substitute available. The alternative opens on a printing or equipment failure and lasts for the emergency period, and workload is neither.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The accessibility duty in § 21 is triggered by ______, reaches ______ on the label, and sets a maximum of ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: the request of an elderly person as defined in section fourteen of chapter nineteen A, or of a person visually impaired; the directions; ten characters per inch.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a pharmacist must produce ten-characters-per-inch directions for any patient who is visibly elderly.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The duty arises upon the request of an elderly person as defined in section fourteen of chapter nineteen A, or of a person visually impaired, not on the pharmacist's assessment of the patient.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: State the recording sequence in 247 CMR 9.04(7) and say what starts it.
retrieval_prompts.answer: It starts whenever a prescription drug has been distributed solely under a generic name. The dispensing pharmacist records the NDC number in the computerized pharmacy system; in the event an NDC number does not exist, the name of the manufacturer; and if the manufacturer's name is not available, the name of the distributor, packer, or repacker.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A generic-only product has no NDC, the manufacturer is named on the carton and the repacker on the invoice. Which name is recorded, and where does it go?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The manufacturer's name, into the computerized pharmacy system. The distributor, packer or repacker becomes available only if the manufacturer's name is not available.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who may receive a new prescription over the telephone under 247 CMR 9.04(8), and on what conditions?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A pharmacy intern, or a certified pharmacy technician who has the approval of the pharmacist on duty, from a prescriber or authorized agent. The technician limb carries both certification and that approval, and 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) adds that the technician must first identify him or herself as a certified pharmacy technician.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the three circumstances in which a pharmacist is not required to distribute the Schedule II and III consumer education pamphlet.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The patient is receiving outpatient palliative care pursuant to section 227 of chapter 111; the patient is a resident of a long-term care facility; or the narcotic or controlled substance is prescribed for use in the treatment of substance use disorder or opioid dependence.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: State the two things M.G.L. c. 94C, § 18D(b) requires of a pharmacist dispensing an opioid contained in Schedule II, and say to whom the second runs.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Inform the patient on the potential adverse risks of the prescription opioid, and offer to dispense an opioid antagonist to the patient and, where applicable, to a designee of the patient, or, for a patient who is a minor, to the minor's parent or guardian.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How does § 18D(a) define an opioid antagonist?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Any drug approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of persons experiencing an opioid overdose.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Schedule II opioid is dispensed to a resident of a long-term care facility. Which of the two duties triggered by that dispensing survives, and why?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The § 18D adverse-risk information and antagonist offer survive. Residence in a long-term care facility is one of the three stated exceptions to the § 21 pamphlet duty, and § 18D states no exception of any kind.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What words close the grant in 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c), and what do they do?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Except where otherwise prohibited by federal or state laws and regulations. They make the certified technician's authority yield to any other federal or state law or regulation prohibiting the act, whatever conditions inside the paragraph are satisfied.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A prescriber's agent telephones a new oral prescription for a controlled substance. Which provision addresses the pharmacist, and what does it require?
retrieval_prompts.answer: M.G.L. c. 94C, § 20(a): upon receiving an oral prescription for a controlled substance from an authorized practitioner, the pharmacist shall immediately reduce the prescription to writing on a prescription form and shall record the information the subsection enumerates.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which category of pharmacy staff is expressly barred from taking prescriptions over the telephone, and under what provision?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A pharmacy technician trainee, under 247 CMR 8.03(4)(c).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: 247 CMR 9.04(8) states the intern limb without an approval condition. What other provision still qualifies how a pharmacy intern works?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 8.01(3): a pharmacy intern shall work under the direct supervision of a registered pharmacist preceptor.

quick_review.text: The § 21 label carries the date of filling, the pharmacy name and address, the filling pharmacist's initials, the prescription serial number, the patient name, the prescriber name, the drug name, directions for use and cautionary statements, and a tablet or capsule count where that is the dosage form.
Inside the § 21 element list the patient's name is the one element stated with an express 'unless': it is required unless it is a veterinary prescription.

A later paragraph of § 21 applies the labeling provisions of that section to the compounding and dispensing of drugs on the oral, electronic or written prescription of a licensed and registered prescriber under section 9, so the label list is not confined to controlled substances.
247 CMR 9.04(3) requires the label affixed to a prescription drug container or package to be clearly printed by a computerized pharmacy system.

The handwritten or typed label in 247 CMR 9.04(3) is available in the event of printing or equipment failure and during an emergency period; legibility is what the substitute must be, not what makes it available.

Upon the request of an elderly person as defined in section fourteen of chapter nineteen A, or of a person visually impaired, the directions on the label shall be typed in a print size allowing no more than ten characters per inch.

Ten characters per inch is a ceiling on character density, it attaches to the directions rather than the whole label, and it is triggered by the request rather than by the pharmacist's view of the patient.
247 CMR 9.04(7) is triggered by distribution solely under a generic name, and it directs the entry into the computerized pharmacy system.

The 247 CMR 9.04(7) sequence runs NDC number, then the manufacturer's name if no NDC number exists, then the distributor, packer or repacker if the manufacturer's name is not available. Each step opens only when the one above it is closed.

Under 247 CMR 9.04(8) a pharmacy intern, or a certified pharmacy technician who has the approval of the pharmacist on duty, may receive new prescriptions over the telephone from a prescriber or authorized agent.

The technician limb of 247 CMR 9.04(8) carries two conditions together, certification and the approval of the pharmacist on duty; the intern limb is stated without the approval qualifier, although 247 CMR 8.01(3) requires a pharmacy intern to work under the direct supervision of a registered pharmacist preceptor.

247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) adds a condition 247 CMR 9.04(8) does not state: a certified pharmacy technician may receive new or omitted prescription information from the prescriber or agent after identifying him or herself as such, and with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.
The same grant in 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) applies except where otherwise prohibited by federal or state laws and regulations, so the conditions inside the paragraph are not the whole test.

M.G.L. c. 94C, § 20(a) addresses the pharmacist as the person who, upon receiving an oral prescription for a controlled substance from an authorized practitioner, shall immediately reduce it to writing on a prescription form and shall record the information the subsection enumerates.
247 CMR 8.03(4)(c): a pharmacy technician trainee may not take prescriptions over the telephone.

A pharmacist shall distribute the consumer education pamphlet when dispensing a narcotic or controlled substance contained in schedule II or III, and the department produces and distributes those pamphlets, in written or electronic form, to pharmacies, not including institutional pharmacies.

The pamphlet is not required where the patient is receiving outpatient palliative care pursuant to section 227 of chapter 111, the patient is a resident of a long-term care facility, or the narcotic or controlled substance is prescribed for use in the treatment of substance use disorder or opioid dependence.

A pharmacist dispensing an opioid contained in Schedule II shall inform the patient on the potential adverse risks of the prescription opioid and shall offer to dispense an opioid antagonist to the patient and, where applicable, to a designee, or for a minor to the parent or guardian.

Section 18D(a) defines an opioid antagonist as any drug approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of persons experiencing an opioid overdose, and § 18D requires an offer rather than acceptance.

decision_logic.condition: A controlled-substance prescription has been filled and the container is about to be labelled.
decision_logic.action: Work the § 21 list in order and check the two conditional items: the patient's name is required unless the prescription is veterinary, and a count is required where the substance is dispensed as tablets or capsules.

decision_logic.condition: A label is about to be produced other than by the pharmacy's computerized system.
decision_logic.action: Ask two questions before accepting it: has there been a printing or equipment failure, and is the pharmacy still inside the emergency period of that failure. If either answer is no, 247 CMR 9.04(3) requires the computerized system regardless of how legible the alternative would be.

decision_logic.condition: A patient appears elderly or appears to have difficulty reading the label.
decision_logic.action: Do nothing on that basis alone. The § 21 duty runs upon the request of an elderly person as defined in section fourteen of chapter nineteen A, or of a person visually impaired, so wait for the request and then type the directions at no more than ten characters per inch.

decision_logic.condition: A product is being dispensed and the question is what identity to record.
decision_logic.action: Ask first whether the drug has been distributed solely under a generic name. If not, 247 CMR 9.04(7) is not engaged. If so, record the NDC number in the computerized pharmacy system; only if none exists, the manufacturer's name; and only if that is unavailable, the distributor, packer or repacker.

decision_logic.condition: A prescriber or authorized agent is on the telephone with a new prescription and the pharmacist is occupied.
decision_logic.action: Ask first what is being telephoned. If it is an oral prescription for a controlled substance, M.G.L. c. 94C, § 20(a) addresses the pharmacist as the person who, upon receiving it, shall immediately reduce it to writing, and the authority 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) gives a certified technician applies only except where otherwise prohibited by federal or state laws and regulations. Otherwise hand the call to a pharmacy intern, who works under the direct supervision of a registered pharmacist preceptor, or to a certified pharmacy technician who identifies herself as such and has the approval of the pharmacist on duty. Confirm certification, confirm that the approval came from the pharmacist on duty rather than from a manager, and do not treat a later check of the transcription as a substitute. A pharmacy technician trainee may not take the call at all.

decision_logic.condition: A narcotic or controlled substance contained in schedule II or III is being dispensed.
decision_logic.action: Distribute the consumer education pamphlet unless one of the three stated exceptions is established on the facts: outpatient palliative care pursuant to section 227 of chapter 111, residence in a long-term care facility, or a prescription for use in the treatment of substance use disorder or opioid dependence.

decision_logic.condition: An opioid contained in Schedule II is being dispensed.
decision_logic.action: Inform the patient on the potential adverse risks of the prescription opioid and offer to dispense an opioid antagonist. Direct the offer to the patient and, where applicable, to a designee, and for a minor patient to the parent or guardian; record no exception, because § 18D states none.

decision_logic.condition: A pamphlet exception has been correctly identified on a Schedule II opioid dispensing.
decision_logic.action: Stop there. The exception disposes of the pamphlet only. Work the § 18D adverse-risk information and antagonist offer separately, because the two duties come from different sections and § 18D carries no exception.

decision_logic.condition: The patient declines the offered opioid antagonist.
decision_logic.action: Treat the duty as discharged by the offer. Section 18D requires the pharmacist to offer to dispense an opioid antagonist, not to secure acceptance, and dispensing the Schedule II opioid is not conditioned on the patient taking one.

ma_vs_federal.text: No federal rule is among this section's dependencies, so no federal standard is stated here. The one federal reference inside the declared scope is a reservation: 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) grants the certified pharmacy technician's authority to request refill authorizations and to receive new or omitted prescription information except where otherwise prohibited by federal or state laws and regulations. What any particular federal provision requires of a telephoned prescription is a separate topic and is not decided here.

exceptions.text: The patient's name is required on the § 21 container label unless it is a veterinary prescription. That is the one element in the list stated with an express 'unless'.
The count of tablets or capsules is conditional rather than excepted: it is required if the controlled substance is dispensed as tablets or capsules, and it has no application to another dosage form.

247 CMR 9.04(3) permits a legibly handwritten or typed prescription label in the event of printing or equipment failure and during an emergency period. Both limbs have to hold; neither workload nor preference opens the exception.

The ten-characters-per-inch standard has no exception stated against it. It is request-triggered rather than excepted, so the absence of a request is a failure of the trigger and not an exemption from a duty already owed.
247 CMR 9.04(7) states no exception to the recording sequence. What varies is which step is reached, and that turns on whether an NDC number exists and whether the manufacturer's name is available.

247 CMR 9.04(8) states no exception of its own. It is a permission with conditions attached, so a technician who lacks certification or the approval of the pharmacist on duty is outside the paragraph rather than inside an exception to it. The reservation on this activity is stated elsewhere, in 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c).

247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) grants the certified pharmacy technician's authority to request refill authorizations and to receive new or omitted prescription information except where otherwise prohibited by federal or state laws and regulations. The reservation sits in the same sentence as the grant, so it can close the authority even where certification, self-identification and the approval of the pharmacist on duty are all in place.

Pharmacists are not required to distribute the pamphlet if the patient is receiving outpatient palliative care pursuant to section 227 of chapter 111, the patient is a resident of a long-term care facility, or the narcotic or controlled substance is prescribed for use in the treatment of substance use disorder or opioid dependence.

Section 18D states no exception at all. In particular it does not except a patient who already keeps an opioid antagonist at home, a patient with prior opioid experience, or a dispensing where the opioid prescriber has not separately ordered an antagonist.

The three pamphlet exceptions belong to the pamphlet. None of them reaches the adverse-risk information or the antagonist offer, so a dispensing may be pamphlet-exempt and still carry both § 18D duties in full.

timing_deadlines.event: Printing or equipment failure in the pharmacy
timing_deadlines.timeframe: During the emergency period of that failure
timing_deadlines.consequence: A prescription label may be legibly handwritten or typed for that period only; once the failure is over, 247 CMR 9.04(3) again requires the label to be clearly printed by a computerized pharmacy system.
The date of filling is itself one of the elements the § 21 label must show, so the label records when the fill happened rather than when the prescription was written.

timing_deadlines.event: Dispensing a narcotic or controlled substance contained in schedule II or III
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pamphlet duty attaches to the act of dispensing, so it is discharged at that point rather than deferred to a later contact with the patient.

timing_deadlines.event: Dispensing an opioid contained in Schedule II
timing_deadlines.consequence: The adverse-risk information and the offer to dispense an opioid antagonist are owed by the pharmacist dispensing the opioid, at that dispensing.

timing_deadlines.event: A new prescription is telephoned to the pharmacy
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At the time the call is received
timing_deadlines.consequence: The certification of the technician, her identification of herself as a certified pharmacy technician and the approval of the pharmacist on duty must already be in place when the call is taken; a review afterwards does not supply any of them.

forms_records.text: The container label is the primary record in this area. Section 21 requires the pharmacist filling a written, electronic or oral prescription for a controlled substance to package the substance in a container and affix to that container a label showing the enumerated elements.

The label identifies the transaction as well as the product: the date of filling, the serial number of the prescription, and the filling pharmacist's initials are all label elements, so the container itself carries who filled it, when, and against which prescription.

Directions for use and cautionary statements go on the label, the cautionary statements being those, if any, contained in the prescription or required by law rather than a set the pharmacist composes at large.

Where the controlled substance is dispensed as tablets or capsules, the number of them in the container is a label element, so the quantity dispensed appears on the container and not only in the pharmacy's own records.

The label is produced by the computerized pharmacy system as a matter of regulation, and the handwritten or typed label is a failure-contingent substitute rather than an alternative format the pharmacy may adopt.
On request, the directions portion of the label is produced to a different specification: typed in a print size allowing no more than ten characters per inch. The rest of the label is unaffected.

The computerized pharmacy system is the record of product identity for a drug distributed solely under a generic name. The entry is the NDC number where one exists, and 247 CMR 9.04(7) names that system specifically rather than the pharmacy's records generally.

Where no NDC number exists, the entry in the computerized pharmacy system is the name of the manufacturer; and where the manufacturer's name is not available, the name of the distributor, packer, or repacker. One identifier is recorded, chosen by position in that sequence.

A new prescription received over the telephone by a pharmacy intern, or by a certified pharmacy technician who has the approval of the pharmacist on duty, enters the pharmacy through that person under 247 CMR 9.04(8); the paragraph governs who may take the call rather than the format of what is written down.

The consumer education pamphlet is produced and distributed by the department, in written or electronic form, to pharmacies, not including institutional pharmacies, and it is the pharmacist who distributes it to the consumer at the qualifying dispensing.

Section 18D describes an exchange rather than a document. What it requires is that the pharmacist inform the patient on the potential adverse risks of the prescription opioid and offer to dispense an opioid antagonist; the section states no form and no separate record of the offer.

role_duties.duty: Package the controlled substance in a container and affix a label showing the date of filling, the pharmacy name and address, the pharmacist's own initials, the prescription serial number, the patient's name unless the prescription is veterinary, the prescriber's name, the drug name, directions and cautionary statements, and a tablet or capsule count where that is the dosage form.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist affixing a label to a container of a prescription drug
role_duties.duty: On the request of an elderly person as defined in section fourteen of chapter nineteen A, or of a person visually impaired, type the directions in a print size allowing no more than ten characters per inch.

Ensure the label affixed to a prescription drug container or package is clearly printed by a computerized pharmacy system, and confine any legibly handwritten or typed label to a printing or equipment failure and to the emergency period of that failure.

Where a prescription drug has been distributed solely under a generic name, record the NDC number in the computerized pharmacy system, or the manufacturer's name if no NDC number exists, or the distributor, packer or repacker if the manufacturer's name is not available.

May receive new prescriptions over the telephone from a prescriber or authorized agent; the intern limb of 247 CMR 9.04(8) is stated without an approval qualifier, and 247 CMR 8.01(3) has the intern working under the direct supervision of a registered pharmacist preceptor.

May receive new prescriptions over the telephone from a prescriber or authorized agent only while certified, only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, and, under 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c), after identifying him or herself as a certified pharmacy technician, that grant applying except where otherwise prohibited by federal or state laws and regulations.
Is the person whose approval 247 CMR 9.04(8) names for the technician limb, so the approval is given by the pharmacist then on duty rather than by a manager or by the pharmacy as an institution.
May not take prescriptions over the telephone, under 247 CMR 8.03(4)(c).

role_duties.role: Pharmacist receiving an oral prescription for a controlled substance
role_duties.duty: M.G.L. c. 94C, § 20(a) addresses the pharmacist as the person who, upon receiving such a prescription from an authorized practitioner, shall immediately reduce it to writing on a prescription form and shall record the information the subsection enumerates.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist dispensing a Schedule II or III narcotic or controlled substance
role_duties.duty: Distribute the consumer education pamphlet, unless the patient is receiving outpatient palliative care pursuant to section 227 of chapter 111, is a resident of a long-term care facility, or the substance is prescribed for use in the treatment of substance use disorder or opioid dependence.
Produce and distribute the consumer pamphlets, either in written or electronic form, to pharmacies, not including institutional pharmacies, covering the topics § 21 enumerates.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist dispensing an opioid contained in Schedule II
role_duties.duty: Inform the patient on the potential adverse risks of the prescription opioid and offer to dispense an opioid antagonist to the patient and, where applicable, to a designee of the patient, or for a minor patient to the minor's parent or guardian.

common_traps.text: Merging the prescription's contents with the label's contents. Section 21 governs what the pharmacist puts on the container, and the prescribing practitioner's registration number is not one of the elements it enumerates.
Treating the tablet or capsule count as an optional courtesy. It is a label element whenever the controlled substance is dispensed as tablets or capsules.

Reading § 21 as a controlled-substance-only provision. A later paragraph applies the labeling provisions to the compounding and dispensing of drugs on the oral, electronic or written prescription of a licensed and registered prescriber under section 9.

Treating a legible handwritten label as always acceptable. Legibility is the standard the substitute label must meet once 247 CMR 9.04(3) opens; a printing or equipment failure and an emergency period are what open it.
Treating a busy period, short staffing or a backlog as the emergency the exception contemplates. The regulation ties the alternative to printing or equipment failure.

Making the accessibility duty automatic for anyone who looks elderly. The statute operates upon the request of an elderly person as defined in section fourteen of chapter nineteen A, or of a person visually impaired.
Reading ten characters per inch as a minimum, or enlarging the whole label. It is a maximum character density, and it attaches to the directions on the label rather than to the label as a whole.

Treating the identifiers in 247 CMR 9.04(7) as interchangeable. They are a ranked sequence, so the distributor, packer or repacker is reached only where no NDC number exists and the manufacturer's name is not available.

Applying 247 CMR 9.04(7) to every dispensing, or discharging it with a paper note. The trigger is a drug distributed solely under a generic name, and the record goes into the computerized pharmacy system.

Assuming that only a pharmacist may take a new telephoned prescription, or that any technician may. A pharmacy intern may, a technician may only if certified and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, and a pharmacy technician trainee may not take the call at all.

Reading 247 CMR 9.04(8) as the whole law on who may take a new telephoned prescription. 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) regulates the same act with a self-identification condition and an express reservation, and M.G.L. c. 94C, § 20(a) addresses the pharmacist where what is telephoned is an oral prescription for a controlled substance.

Treating the conditions inside 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) as the whole test. The same sentence grants the authority except where otherwise prohibited by federal or state laws and regulations, so satisfying every condition in the paragraph does not answer whether another law closes it.

Accepting a later pharmacist check, or a manager's standing policy, in place of the approval of the pharmacist on duty. The approval conditions who may receive the call, and it cannot be supplied after the call has been taken.

Assuming every Schedule II or III dispensing requires the pamphlet, without checking the three statutory exceptions against the facts, or stating the first of them without its cross-reference to section 227 of chapter 111.
Turning an obligation to inform and offer into a requirement that the patient accept or purchase an opioid antagonist, or conditioning the offer on the prescriber having ordered one.
Reading a patient's minority as a reason the antagonist offer falls away. Section 18D routes the offer to the minor's parent or guardian instead.

Carrying a pamphlet exception across to § 18D. The two duties are triggered by the same dispensing but stated in different sections, and § 18D contains no exception for palliative care, long-term care residency or a substance use disorder indication.

drug_examples.teaching_point: Oxycodone is a Schedule II opioid, so a single dispensing sits inside both counter duties at once: the pharmacist distributes the consumer education pamphlet unless one of the three stated exceptions applies, and separately informs the patient on the potential adverse risks and offers to dispense an opioid antagonist. Establishing a pamphlet exception disposes of the pamphlet only.

Buprenorphine and naloxone dispensed in Schedule III for the treatment of opioid use disorder is inside the pamphlet trigger and inside a stated exception to it, because the substance is prescribed for use in the treatment of substance use disorder or opioid dependence. It is outside § 18D altogether, which reaches an opioid contained in Schedule II.

Naloxone is an opioid antagonist within the § 18D(a) definition, being approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of persons experiencing an opioid overdose. What § 18D requires of the pharmacist is the offer to dispense one; the pathways by which an antagonist is actually supplied are a separate subject.

Alprazolam is a controlled substance in Schedule IV, which places a dispensing of it squarely inside the § 21 label list: where it is dispensed as tablets, the number of tablets in the container is a label element alongside the date of filling, the filling pharmacist's initials and the serial number of the prescription. The label list turns on the substance being controlled, not on its being Schedule II or III.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws c. 94C

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: When a pharmacist fills a controlled-substance prescription, Massachusetts law requires the dispensing container label to include the statutory information such as fill date, pharmacy name and address, pharmacist initials, prescription serial number, patient name when applicable, prescriber, drug, directions and required cautionary statements, plus tablet or capsule count when applicable.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A licensee shall ensure the label affixed to a prescription drug container or package is CLEARLY PRINTED BY A COMPUTERIZED PHARMACY SYSTEM. In the event of printing or equipment failure, a prescription label may be legibly handwritten or typed DURING AN EMERGENCY PERIOD. The alternative is tied to a failure and to a period, not to convenience.
exceptions: Legibly handwritten or typed during an emergency period of printing or equipment failure

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: UPON THE REQUEST of an elderly person, as defined in M.G.L. c. 19A, s. 14, or of a person who is VISUALLY IMPAIRED, the directions on the label affixed by the pharmacist to a container of a prescription drug shall be TYPED IN A PRINT SIZE ALLOWING NO MORE THAN TEN CHARACTERS PER INCH. The duty is triggered by the request, and the standard is expressed as a maximum character density rather than a point size.

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Whenever a prescription drug has been distributed SOLELY UNDER A GENERIC NAME, the dispensing pharmacist shall record the NDC number in the computerized pharmacy system. In the event an NDC number does not exist, the pharmacist shall record the NAME OF THE MANUFACTURER, or, if the manufacturer's name is not available, the name of the DISTRIBUTOR, PACKER, OR REPACKER. The fallbacks run in that order.

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A pharmacy intern, or a CERTIFIED pharmacy technician WHO HAS THE APPROVAL OF THE PHARMACIST ON DUTY, may receive NEW prescriptions over the telephone from a prescriber or an authorized agent. Both limbs matter for the technician: certification and the on-duty pharmacist's approval.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws c. 94C

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Massachusetts requires the designated consumer educational pamphlet when a pharmacy dispenses a narcotic or controlled substance in Schedule II or III, subject to statutory exceptions including outpatient palliative care, long-term-care residents, and treatment of substance use disorder or opioid dependence.
exceptions: Outpatient palliative care; resident of a long-term care facility; drug prescribed for substance use disorder or opioid-dependence treatment.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws c. 94C

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: When a pharmacist dispenses an opioid contained in Schedule II, Massachusetts law requires the pharmacist to inform the patient of the potential adverse risks of the prescription opioid and to offer to dispense an opioid antagonist to the patient and, where applicable, a designee; for a minor patient, the offer is made to the parent or guardian.
exceptions: Section 18D does not state an exception based on prior opioid experience, possession of an opioid antagonist at home, or absence of a separate antagonist prescription from the opioid prescriber.

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 8.04(4)(c) a certified pharmacy technician, after identifying him or herself as such, may request refill authorizations from the prescriber or the prescriber's agent and, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, receive new or omitted prescription information, including communicating information recorded on a patient profile that does not require professional judgment or interpretation. Under 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) a certified pharmacy technician may, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, perform prescription transfers between pharmacies for Schedule VI controlled substances only. Under 247 CMR 8.04(4)(e) a certified pharmacy technician may not administer medications or vaccines, perform drug utilization review, conduct clinical conflict resolution, contact prescribers about therapy clarification or modification, provide patient counseling, or perform final dispensing process validation.

learning_objectives: State the four core verbs of the statutory definition of collaborative drug therapy management and distinguish them from the activities the definition merely may include.

orientation.text: Collaborative drug therapy management is defined in M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a) as the initiating, monitoring, modifying and discontinuing of a patient's drug therapy by a pharmacist in accordance with a collaborative practice agreement. Those four verbs are the whole of the core definition, and each of them operates only through the agreement. The definition then adds three things the practice may include, and they are not equally conditioned. Collecting and reviewing patient histories, and obtaining and checking vital signs including pulse, temperature, blood pressure and respiration, are stated without any attached condition. The laboratory limb is stated with three conditions at once: the pharmacist acts under the supervision of, or in direct consultation with, a physician; the work is performed in accordance with approved protocols applicable to the practice setting; and the evaluation shall not include a diagnostic component. The last of those is the boundary of the whole authority. Satisfying the conditions for ordering a test does nothing to enlarge what the pharmacist's evaluation of the result may conclude, so a properly ordered test does not license a diagnosis drawn from it.

Who may collaborate is settled before any of that, and it is settled by three instruments that do not say the same thing. M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(b) lists six things a pharmacist shall do or have in order to enter into a collaborative practice agreement. The pharmacist shall hold a current licence to practise pharmacy in the commonwealth and currently be engaged in pharmacy practice in the commonwealth, which is two requirements in one clause and not one. The pharmacist shall have at least 1,000,000 dollars of professional liability insurance. The pharmacist shall have earned a doctor of pharmacy degree or have completed five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist or the equivalent, which the statute states as alternatives rather than cumulatively. The pharmacist shall agree to devote a portion of practice to the defined drug therapy area to be co-managed, and shall agree to complete, in each year of the agreement, at least five additional contact hours or 0.5 continuing education units of board-approved continuing education addressing areas of practice generally related to collaborative practice agreements. The sixth element is conditional rather than absolute: the pharmacist shall apply to participate in the medical assistance program for the limited purpose of ordering and referring covered services if regulations governing that limited participation are promulgated under chapter 118E. Answer a question framed on the statute from those words, but do not stop there, because a pharmacist who is actually going to practise has to satisfy the regulations as well, and neither 247 CMR 16.02(1) nor 243 CMR 2.12(2) stops where the statute does.

247 CMR 16.02(1) is the Board of Registration in Pharmacy's version of the same list, and it governs a pharmacist who wants to qualify to enter into a collaborative practice agreement and engage in collaborative practice. Its licence element, 247 CMR 16.02(1)(a), is a current unrestricted license in good standing to practice pharmacy in the Commonwealth together with current engagement in Massachusetts pharmacy practice, so a pharmacist practising under a live restriction fails it while holding a licence that is perfectly current. Its insurance element, 247 CMR 16.02(1)(b), is at least $1,000,000 per occurrence of professional liability insurance, maintained during the term of the agreement, which specifically covers drug therapy management; an aggregate-only policy, a policy that lapses mid-term and a general pharmacist policy that does not reach drug therapy management each fail it with the right figure on the page. The credential element is the one that decides fact patterns. 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) requires five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist unless the pharmacist has satisfied one of the requirements in 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c)1. through 2. Subparagraph 1. is a doctor of pharmacy degree and a collaborative practice agreement entered on or before June 30, 2017, both limbs together. Subparagraph 2. is such other education or residency criteria as the Board determines to be the equivalent of five years experience. So a pharmacist entering an agreement today cannot reach the element on the degree alone: that route is closed by its own date, and what is left is the five years or a Board determination of equivalence. The continuing-education element, 247 CMR 16.02(1)(e), is five additional contact hours of Board-approved continuing education in each year of the term, with no continuing education unit alternative stated, addressing areas of practice generally related to the particular collaborative practice agreement. 247 CMR 16.02(1)(f) adds further conditions, but only where prescriptive practices are included in the agreement, and those belong to the separate section on prescribing.

It would be a mistake to treat 247 CMR 16.02 as the Board of Registration in Pharmacy's private business. 243 CMR 2.12(1) defines an Authorized Pharmacist as a pharmacist who is currently registered by the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and is in good standing, who meets the requirements of 247 CMR 16.02, and who is participating in drug therapy management with a supervising physician pursuant to a written agreement with written protocols. The three limbs are stated together, so a pharmacist who does not meet 247 CMR 16.02 is not an authorized pharmacist for the Board of Registration in Medicine's purposes either. That board nevertheless keeps its own qualification list, and it is not identical. 243 CMR 2.12(2)(a) and (b) state the licence and insurance elements in the same words the pharmacy regulation uses. But 243 CMR 2.12(2)(c) states the credential element as the statute does, a doctor of pharmacy degree or five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist, with no date attached to the degree; and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(e) keeps the five contact hours or 0.5 continuing education units alternative while tying the subject matter, as the pharmacy regulation does, to the particular agreement. When a question gives you a pharmacist who holds the degree but not the years, read which instrument the question is asking about: the statute and 243 CMR 2.12(2)(c) are answered by the degree alone, and 247 CMR 16.02(1)(c) is not. For a pharmacist actually proposing to practise, the narrower provision is the operative one, because 243 CMR 2.12(1) makes meeting 247 CMR 16.02 part of what it is to be an authorized pharmacist.

Where collaborative practice may happen is a closed list with a different approving body attached to each entry, and the single most common error in this area is to carry one approval across all of them. Under M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(c)(1) through (4), a hospital licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 51 requires approval by the medical staff executive committee at the licensed hospital or a designee; a long-term care facility licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 71 requires approval by the facility's medical director or a designee; an inpatient or outpatient hospice setting licensed under M.G.L. c. 111, § 57D requires approval by the hospice's medical director or a designee; and an ambulatory care clinic requires approval by the clinic's medical staff executive committee or designee, or its medical director or designee. The ambulatory care clinic carries a condition none of the other three does, and it is cumulative with approval rather than an alternative to it: collaborative practice there is allowed with on-site supervision by the attending physician and a collaborating pharmacist. Note also that the hospital limb and the ambulatory care clinic limb both rest on the same licensing provision, M.G.L. c. 111, § 51, so a difference in licensing section is not what separates them. These four limbs are the ones this section teaches; collaborative practice by a pharmacist in a retail drug business is dealt with by a separate section.

Employment is regulated by purpose, not by the bare fact of a hiring, and the direction of the hiring matters. M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(e) permits a physician or a physician group to hire pharmacists for the purpose of practising collaborative drug therapy management under an agreement for the benefit of a patient of that physician or physician group. Running the same arrangement the other way is where the bar falls: no retail pharmacy may employ a physician for the purpose of maintaining, establishing or entering into a collaborative practice agreement with a patient. The same subsection then preserves an engagement that looks superficially similar, providing that nothing shall prohibit a retail pharmacy from hiring a physician or licensed medical practitioner for the purpose of conducting quality assurance reviews of its pharmacists engaged in the practice of collaborative drug therapy. The implementing regulation, 247 CMR 16.04(7), states the same three propositions in its own order -- the permission at (a), the quality-assurance saving at (b) and the prohibition at (c) -- with one difference of vocabulary worth noticing: where the statute says retail pharmacy, 247 CMR 16.04(7)(b) and (c) say community pharmacy. The two instruments are describing the same setting under different labels, so a fact pattern that uses either word is asking about the same rule. One further difference of wording is worth noting rather than worrying about: the statute closes its prohibition with the words with a patient and 247 CMR 16.04(7)(c) does not, but both turn on the purpose of the employment rather than on the fact of it.

Before asking whether a supervising physician has become ineligible, ask what made him eligible in the first place, because the regulation states a positive requirement and not merely a list of disqualifications. Under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(a) a physician must possess an active license to practice medicine issued by the Board and must be actively engaged in the clinical practice of medicine and the provision of patient care in the particular field of medicine in which the collaborative drug therapy management is to take place. That is two things again, and the second is field-specific: a licensed physician who has left clinical practice, or who is in active practice but in a different field from the therapy to be co-managed, does not satisfy it. 243 CMR 2.12(3)(b) then fixes the relationship. The physician is the supervisor in the agreement and retains the ultimate responsibility for the care of the patient, and in a community pharmacy setting a physician should enter into only as many agreements as he or she can reasonably and safely supervise at one time. And 243 CMR 2.12(3)(c) puts a documentary duty on the physician: the supervising physician shall assess the patient and make a written referral of the identified patient to the authorized pharmacist, and that written referral shall include a primary diagnosis and any co-morbid conditions that are included in the collaborative management. 243 CMR 2.12(3)(c) states that duty without confining it to one practice setting, which is worth holding beside the setting-sensitive definition of Referral taken up further below.

A collaboration can also fail from the physician's side, and it can fail silently. Under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(d) a physician is ineligible to participate in collaborative drug therapy management if he or she is in a Voluntary Agreement Not to Practice Medicine with the Board, or has had a licence to practise medicine temporarily suspended or revoked by the Board. Separately, a physician shall be deemed ineligible if he or she has voluntarily surrendered, or has had suspended, revoked or restricted, a controlled substances licence, permit or registration, either state or federal. That second sentence is the one that catches people out, because it turns on a registration rather than on the medical licence, it reaches a federal event as readily as a state one, and it reaches a mere restriction as well as a surrender or revocation. The same provision allows the Board to revoke a physician's right to participate in a collaborative agreement on any of the grounds for discipline in 243 CMR 1.03(5). Notice is not the trigger. Under 243 CMR 2.12(3)(e), where the Board enters into a Voluntary Agreement Not to Practice with a licensee, summarily suspends a licence, or takes final disciplinary action by final decision and order or by approving a consent agreement, the Board may require the physician to give written notification to each authorized pharmacist with whom he or she is in an agreement. That is a discretion, so the absence of notice tells the pharmacist nothing about whether the authority still exists.

Eligibility of the patient is a separate gate, and it sits upstream of every clinical act. The definition of patient in M.G.L. c. 112, § 24B1/2(a) is a person who is referred to a pharmacist by his supervising physician for the purpose of receiving collaborative drug therapy management services from the pharmacist. A person who asks for the service, or who reports that a physician mentioned it, is not yet a patient within the definition. The definition then loads three further duties onto that one sentence. The supervising physician shall assess the patient and include a diagnosis when referring the patient to the collaborating pharmacist, so a referral carrying no diagnosis is incomplete on its face. The patient shall be notified of, and shall consent to, the services in the retail drug business setting, which is a setting-specific requirement rather than a universal one. And individual referral and consent shall be recorded by the pharmacist and the supervising physician in the patient's record, which binds both professionals; an entry made by the physician alone does not discharge the pharmacist's duty, and an entry made by the pharmacist alone does not discharge the physician's.

The word referral does not mean the same thing everywhere, and this is the point at which identical facts produce opposite answers in two settings. Under 243 CMR 2.12(1), Referral means the individual patient referral by a supervising physician to an authorized pharmacist for the purpose of receiving collaborative services in a community pharmacy setting; in all other practice settings, Referral means the consultation of a supervising physician and an authorized pharmacist about a patient for that purpose. So a conversation between a physician and a pharmacist about a named patient can itself be the referral in a hospital, a long-term care facility, a hospice or an ambulatory care clinic, while the same conversation in a community pharmacy is not one. In the community pharmacy setting the supervising physician shall execute a written referral, and 243 CMR 2.12(1) lists what it shall include without limiting it to those items: the patient's name and address, the primary diagnosis for which the services are authorized, the diagnosis of any comorbid conditions for which they are authorized, any known patient drug allergies, a statement that the patient has executed a written consent, and any other specific instructions to the authorized pharmacist. Two of the named items are easy to leave out, the allergies and the statement about consent, and a referral that is signed, detailed and specific is still incomplete without them. Keep the definition separate from the physician's own duty: 243 CMR 2.12(1) tells you what counts as a Referral in each setting, while 243 CMR 2.12(3)(c) separately requires the supervising physician to assess the patient and make a written referral of the identified patient carrying a primary diagnosis and any co-morbid conditions included in the collaborative management, and states that duty without a setting limit. So a consultation in a hospital is a Referral within the definition without discharging the physician's own writing duty.

It is worth fixing what this section does not reach, because collaborative practice is split across several sections and the boundaries are drawn by subject rather than by instrument. This section covers the entry conditions only: what collaborative drug therapy management is and where its diagnostic boundary falls, which pharmacists qualify under the statute and under each board's regulation, which settings allow the practice and who approves it in each, who may employ whom, what makes a supervising physician eligible and when he stops being eligible, who counts as a patient, and what a referral is in each setting. What the collaborative practice agreement itself must contain, how it is renewed, filed, delegated under and terminated, is the subject of a separate section. What a pharmacist may actually prescribe, modify or discontinue once the agreement is in place is the subject of another. The distinct regime that governs the retail drug business setting, including its own scope limits on patients, diseases and drug therapy, is the subject of a third. When a question turns on any of those, the answer is not in the material below, and reasoning from the entry conditions to a conclusion about agreement terms or prescribing powers is the wrong move.
